item.title: As usual, sorry for necro
item.content:encoded:
Definitely +1, amazingly written story, though I personally don't care for the picture that much, but I get the similarity to 106 and that's kinda cool.

Questions / criticism:
What's up with the hole in the skull of that one soldier and the stuffed-in tongue? Just a messed up game that 106 plays?

Same question about the teeth.

What's up with the rats? That doesn't really seem to be connected to 106, does it?

As others have pointed out, it's weird that Lawrence was kind of 106 before the hole. And that there was 106 activity in that nightmare trench before he got there. Though I personally think that this is a major part of what makes this story so great and leaves some nice room for the reader.

Something that bothered me was the lack of paperwork. Just doesn't really add up. Wouldn't people be all the more careful regarding his documents, once they realized there weren't any previous ones? Like, if I am the commander of that squad and I send 'dat weird guy' away, wouldn't I be like 'make sure they're getting his papers, it was really weird for us when he got here and didn't have any, I don't think that the higher ups would be amused if I couldn't account for one of my soldiers, etc.'

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Holy… halp.

Begins to imagine the scenes in horrific detail.

Ahh, no, stop.

Begins to imagine 106 pulling out the teeth of the men, the ooze dissolving their very gums and screaming agony.

AHH, STOP, NO, AAHHH!

God, I love this, in an extremely unsettling way, that has nothing to do with love. The rats that do not go away, the gruesome deaths, the ooze and the slime and the rot and the sludge (amazing word choice all the way through, by the way), the unsettling happiness of 106, especially with the picture, just beautiful, in a very, very grotesque way that is not beautiful at all.

Corporal Lawrence's joviality is especially unsettling. I mean:

The corporal would rant quietly to the other patients, whispers about endless halls, pursuits in the dark, flesh laid out like pages of a book.

Jesus… I now have an amazing new fascination with 106, because, for me, the most interesting part about 106 is the sheer sickening glee, even felicity, with which he murders people, or… does things to them beyond where the imagination would like to roam, he is the epitamy of the eldritch horror that murders and tortures for fun. And this gives that side of it a HUGE boost for me; he wasn't always like this (although he wasn't exactly normal in the first place), that pit did something to him, made him be like that. The unnaturalness is glorious.

I mostly adore the bit in the German trench. For me that is just the best part because it's the most unexplained. The Germans dug something up, and it, just… I don't know. Was there anything actually there, where did it go? If not, how did they die? What the hell happened to Corporal Lawrence and the German soldiers? Who the hell was Corporal Lawrence?! Was he special in some way for the pit to 'claim' him? What happened to the pit, and the German trench afterwards, did they fill it in, is it still there?! This is the kind of Lovecraftian stuff I adore: very creepy and graphic, but most of all, unexplained and unknown.

item.content:encoded:
Well, I have a funny theory now. No canon and all that, I'm just having fun.

+ show block
– hide block

106 is the pocket dimension. The old man, Corporal Lawrence, is a channel. A tool for the dimension to cause the pain it causes, because it's what it does best. The dimension itself cannot seep into this world without a channel; that is, a person. But of course it seems that the dimension itself, the rot that it is made of, has a rather unbecoming effect on its own physical manifestation on this world.

The haunted trench was its last opus before it had to retire itself before its previous channel decayed into a pile of pure rot itself. The opening was left for an unsuspecting new channel to find and become the dimension's hand in our world and continue its glorious work.

The good news, then, is that The Old Man will eventually die and become an easily containable hole. The bad news, though, is that no one knows when, and even then we know that there is really no way to kill it. Just pray no one finds it again.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I just realized something.

106 is often called Radical Larry. Larry is the shortened form of the name "Lawrence". And what's the name of the Young Man in this tale? Corporal Lawrence. To take it one step further: "radical" is a synonym for "bottom", and Corporal is pretty near the bottom of the military ranking system, only one rank above private.

So, whether intentionally or not… Radical Larry is kind of canon now.

Very good. I do have a few grammar/word critiques:

They moved fast and low, from crater to crater, slipping over slick mud and barbed wire

Shouldn't that be "under the barbed wire"?

More remains were found, each seemingly more unsettling and strange than the last.

Get rid of "seemingly". Both "unsettling" and "strange" are matters of personal reaction.

No more than four feet across, it seemed to be the accidental uncovering of a natural chamber,

I think that would be better as "it seemed to have accidentally uncovered a natural chamber".

item.content:encoded: At first I liked this, but the more I thought about this the more I really just wasn't sure. My beef with it is it really doesn't make sense. Lawrence falls into a hole which makes him into 106, yes? Then what destroyed the German trench, and why did he seem to have 106-y decay powers beforehand? And if he was an anomaly beforehand, what was the significance of the hole? Did Lawrence kill Private Dixon? I really enjoyed the way this was written, and I feel that this is a good origin story of SCP-106, but I also think that some things could be explained a bit better.
